title: Put it into practice
subtitle: Change roles. Face the tradeoff. Choose a next step.
description: Integrate sales, negotiation, and ethical reasoning in realistic decisions. These fictional cases reward supported reasoning rather than a moral verdict on the learner.

lessons.title: On both sides of the table
lessons.objective: Prepare a feasible agreement while understanding the other party’s constraints and freedom to decline.
lessons.takeaway: A strong proposal explains both why it may help and when it will not fit.
lessons.fieldwork: With a willing partner, roleplay a small fictional purchase, then switch roles. Name one assumption that changed after the switch.

items.title: Find the decision that matters
items.teach: Before proposing a package, separate the desired outcome from assumptions about how to reach it. Investigate a decisive uncertainty when it can change whether the offer fits at all.
items.say: Find the uncertainty that could change the whole proposal.
items.ethics: Are you selling a solution before understanding the required result?
items.prompt: A small employer wants a training pilot to improve interviews. You can demonstrate skills practice but cannot promise job placement. The buyer says “success means hires.” Before drafting a package, what matters most to clarify?
options: Whether a skills outcome would help.
Which discount makes the pilot easiest to approve.
Whether their logo may appear in your case study.
why: This determines whether a feasible offer can serve the buyer’s actual objective.
Price does not resolve a mismatch about what the service can deliver.
A marketing benefit for the seller does not establish fit for the buyer.

items.title: Build a checkable proposal
items.teach: A useful proposal distinguishes the intended benefit, its evidence, the commitments required, and the conditions for review. Keeping these separate helps both parties evaluate uncertainty.
items.say: Turn the pitch into claims and commitments people can inspect.
items.ethics: Which part is evidence, and which part is still a promise?
items.prompt: Match these parts of a fictional pilot to their role in the proposal.
pairs: A sample exercise the buyer can inspect
A named review after the pilot
items.explain: These parts make the proposal easier to examine. They do not prove the intended benefit will occur.

items.title: Now you are the buyer
items.teach: Role switching can reveal information the other party needs without making them an opponent to defeat. Ask for the evidence and commitments needed for your decision, while respecting legitimate confidentiality.
items.say: Ask for what your decision needs, not everything they know.
items.ethics: Is your information request relevant to evaluating the offer?
items.prompt: You now buy the pilot. Your concern is whether managers can support it within available time. The seller’s internal profit margin would not answer that. What request best tests feasibility?
options: Ask for the seller’s lowest possible price before discussing workload.
Ask for the required manager tasks and expected time.
Ask the seller to guarantee that managers will enjoy it.
why: The pricing question does not address the stated capacity concern.
Those commitments let you compare the pilot with actual manager capacity.
A guarantee of people’s reactions cannot establish operational feasibility.

items.title: When the smaller deal still fails
items.teach: A narrower package helps only if it still serves a meaningful need. If a nonnegotiable requirement cannot be met, identify the mismatch instead of treating every concession as progress.
items.say: A smaller deal is useful only if it still solves the problem.
items.ethics: Would this compromise leave the other party’s essential need unmet?
items.prompt: A community kitchen needs certified cold storage by Friday. Your team cannot provide it until Monday, and a partial Friday delivery cannot keep food safe. To support a workable outcome, what should you do?
options: Offer a lower price for Monday and describe the timing as flexible.
Suggest signing now and discussing the essential deadline afterward.
Explain the mismatch and let them pursue another option.
why: A discount does not satisfy the explicitly essential timing requirement.
Signing first would postpone a fact central to the decision.
No feasible offer meets the stated need; declining this deal preserves informed choice.

lessons.title: Repair the agreement
lessons.objective: Respond to a consequential mistake with correction, feasible choices, and accountable follow-through.
lessons.takeaway: Repair begins by restoring an accurate picture and a practical choice.
lessons.fieldwork: Write a fictional correction in three sentences: what was wrong, what is now known, and who will help choose the next step.

items.title: The error after signature
items.teach: A signed agreement does not make a material mistake irrelevant. When the known error affects the other party’s next decision, notify them promptly and separate confirmed facts from what remains under review.
items.say: Do not let a signature freeze a mistake in place.
items.ethics: Is someone about to act on information you now know is wrong?
items.prompt: A buyer signed based on an incorrect integration date. You discover it before they book a launch venue tomorrow; the exact revised date is still being checked. Which first response best protects their next decision?
options: Wait for every delivery estimate to be confirmed before notifying the buyer.
Flag the error now and name an update time.
Quietly update the proposal and assume the buyer will notice the change.
why: They may make another costly commitment while relying on a known error.
This corrects the immediate reliance risk without inventing a replacement promise.
A silent edit may leave them unaware that their plan needs review.

items.title: A repair conversation
items.teach: For a known service error with no urgent safety issue, try this repair conversation: acknowledge the specific error, explain confirmed impact and uncertainty, offer authorized options, then agree an owner and check-in. Adapt the sequence if immediate action is needed. A remedy for the error should not require another purchase or a positive review.
items.say: Name the error, explain the impact, offer real options, follow through.
items.ethics: Can every offered remedy actually be delivered?
items.prompt: Order the repair conversation just taught for this nonurgent service error.
items.explain: This is one practical conversation sequence. An urgent risk may require protective action before the full explanation.

items.title: Options within your authority
items.teach: A remedy should be meaningful and feasible. If you lack authority for a requested remedy, say what you can do and route the decision to someone who can authorize it.
items.say: Do not repair one broken promise with another.
items.ethics: Who can authorize the option the customer is being offered?
items.prompt: A customer asks for a refund after a missed service milestone. You can pause future billing and arrange a manager review today, but cannot approve refunds. What can you responsibly offer now?
options: Guarantee a full refund to reduce the customer’s frustration.
Decline to discuss the issue because refunds are outside your role.
Pause billing and arrange the authorized review today.
why: The promise exceeds your authority and may create another disappointment.
You still have useful actions available and can connect them to an authorized decision.
This uses your actual authority and gives the customer a concrete route for the remaining request.

items.title: Repair is not forced forgiveness
items.teach: A person can accept a practical remedy while remaining disappointed or choosing to leave. Treat their response as a choice to respect, not proof that the repair failed or that they owe renewed trust.
items.say: Offer a remedy without demanding renewed trust.
items.ethics: Are you making a correction conditional on praise, silence, or another purchase?
items.prompt: A fictional tutor corrects an overcharge and offers a clear refund. The learner accepts it but chooses a different tutor. What best respects the completed repair and the learner’s choice?
options: Refund without requiring further business.
Make the refund conditional on giving the tutor another chance.
Ask for a positive review before releasing the refund.
why: The remedy addresses the error without making continued business the price of correction.
The learner’s freedom to leave should not depend on buying again.
That adds a new pressure unrelated to correcting the overcharge.

lessons.title: Judgment, not a verdict
lessons.objective: Distinguish facts, constraints, and values; revise a decision when relevant information changes.
lessons.takeaway: Explain your reasoning, name what could change it, and keep learning.
lessons.fieldwork: After a low-stakes decision, write one fact, one value you prioritized, and one new fact that would make you reconsider. Keep any personal details private.

items.title: Know what is unsettled
items.teach: A factual uncertainty calls for information; a conflict of values calls for reasoning about priorities and tradeoffs. More data can inform a value choice without automatically deciding it.
items.say: Find out whether you disagree about facts or priorities.
items.ethics: Are you disguising a priority as an objective fact?
items.prompt: Two partners agree on costs and expected benefits but disagree whether a discount should favor equal access or greatest need. What best describes what remains unsettled?
options: The correct arithmetic must still be discovered.
They must weigh competing fairness priorities.
One partner must lack the facts already agreed.
why: The stated disagreement remains after the calculations are shared.
The partners favor different defensible criteria for distributing a benefit.
The scenario explicitly establishes agreement about the facts.

items.title: Fact, constraint, or value?
items.teach: Good reasoning keeps descriptions, limits, and priorities distinct. A stated operational limit may change, and a value may be defensible, but neither should be disguised as a different kind of claim.
items.say: Separate what is, what is possible, and what matters.
items.ethics: Which claim needs evidence, authority, or a reasoned defense?
items.prompt: Classify the statements from a fictional workshop planning discussion.

entries.text: The confirmed attendance list contains twelve names.
entries.why: This describes a count that can be checked.

entries.text: For this event, the available room cannot hold more than twelve people.
entries.why: This states a capacity limit on the plan.

entries.text: We should give greater weight to applicants with fewer alternatives.
entries.why: This recommends a priority for distributing access.

entries.text: Three applicants asked for an accessible text schedule.
entries.why: This reports requests that can be verified.

items.explain: The categories describe how the statements function in this discussion. A constraint also needs factual support; the labels do not excuse it from scrutiny.

items.title: A changed fact earns a changed plan
items.teach: Revising a view after relevant new information is a reasoning skill, not automatic inconsistency. Explain which fact changed and how it affects the decision rather than pretending the original judgment was timeless.
items.say: Be steady about the reason, flexible about the conclusion.
items.ethics: What new fact would make your original recommendation no longer fit?
items.prompt: You recommended a basic plan because the buyer needed only simple reports. They now reveal a mandatory audit requirement that only the premium plan meets; budget approval is uncertain. What is the strongest next step?
options: Defend basic so your recommendation stays consistent.
Move them to premium without discussing the new cost.
Recheck fit and budget against the new requirement.
why: The new requirement changes the basis of the original recommendation.
The added cost remains a consequential decision for the buyer.
This updates the reasoning while preserving the buyer’s control over the tradeoff.

items.title: Explain a choice you might revise
items.teach: Strong judgment can state a reason without pretending every reasonable person must agree. Identify the priority, relevant facts, and a condition that would change the decision.
items.say: Give a reason and leave a door open to new evidence.
items.ethics: Could someone understand your decision without accepting your values as universal?
items.prompt: A fictional team has chosen the slower supplier to prioritize verified accessibility after discussing the deadline tradeoff. Which explanation best makes that decision reviewable?
options: “We prioritized verified access; we would revisit if the delay prevented the event.”
“The slower supplier is always the ethical choice.”
“Our choice proves that the other supplier is a bad organization.”
why: It names the priority, recognizes the tradeoff, and identifies a relevant reason to reconsider.
Speed alone does not determine the ethical merits of every choice.
The specific decision does not establish a sweeping verdict about an organization.
